label: Sharp interlocking teeth and tusks never occur together
claim: No animal that has sharp, interlocking (saw-like) teeth also has tusks; tusks go to animals that strike in fighting and saw-teeth to those that bite.
quote: No animal that has sharp interfitting teeth is at the same time furnished with tusks. For nature never makes anything superfluous or in vain.
scope: mammals with tusks (e.g. swine) and saw-toothed animals (e.g. wild carnivores)
measurable_quantities: co-occurrence of tusks and interlocking carnassial/sectorial dentition across mammal taxa
candidate_data: Comparative dental morphology in MorphoSource specimens and Phenoscape character matrices, with taxa placed on the Open Tree of Life.

label: Nature gives each weapon only, or most fully, to animals that can use it
claim: Nature allots each offensive or defensive weapon (sting, spur, horn, tusk) only, or in a more developed form, to the animals that can use it, and in its most perfect form to those that can use it best.
quote: Nature allots each weapon, offensive and defensive alike, to those animals alone that can use it; or, if not to them alone, to them in a more marked degree; and she allots it in its most perfect state to those that can use it best
candidate_data: none known

label: Weapons such as horns and spurs are confined to or larger in males
claim: Because males are stronger and more spirited than females, weapons such as horns, tusks and spurs are found only in males in some species and are more fully developed in males in others (e.g. stags have horns and hinds none; hens often lack the spurs of cocks).
quote: Thus as males are stronger and more choleric than females, it is in males that such parts as those just mentioned are found, either exclusively, as in some species, or more fully developed, as in others.
scope: animals with horns, tusks or spurs: deer, cattle, sheep, spurred birds
measurable_quantities: presence and size of horns, antlers, tusks and spurs in males versus females of each species
candidate_data: Sexual-dimorphism trait data in the Animal Diversity Web and the Amniote Life-History Database, with antler/horn presence by sex from bovid and cervid species accounts.

label: All fishes have saw-like teeth except the parrot-fish (Scarus)
claim: All fishes have sharp, serrated (saw-like) teeth, with the single exception of the Scarus (parrot-fish).
quote: All fishes have teeth of the serrated form, with the single exception of the fish known as the Scarus.
scope: fishes; Scarus (parrot-fish, Sparisoma cretense in the Mediterranean)
measurable_quantities: tooth shape (sharp/conical versus flat/grinding or fused) across fish species
candidate_data: Dentition and diet fields in FishBase, plus fish skull scans in MorphoSource.

label: Hook-clawed birds have hooked beaks and eat no vegetable food
claim: Birds with crooked talons (birds of prey) invariably have a hooked beak, because they are carnivorous and eat no vegetable food at all.
quote: Thus in those birds that are called Crooked-clawed it is invariably hooked, inasmuch as these birds are carnivorous, and eat no kind of vegetable food whatsoever.
measurable_quantities: beak curvature
fraction of plant matter in diet
candidate_data: Beak measurements and trophic niche in AVONET, and diet composition in EltonTraits.

label: True horns occur only in viviparous animals
claim: True horns exist only in viviparous animals; what are called horns in some egg-laying animals are horns only by metaphor and are never used for fighting.
quote: They exist in none but viviparous animals; though in some ovipara certain parts are metaphorically spoken of as horns, in virtue of a certain resemblance.
scope: viviparous animals (mammals) versus egg-laying animals (reptiles, birds, fishes, insects)
measurable_quantities: presence of horn-like head appendages and their use in combat across taxa
candidate_data: Anatomy and behaviour accounts in the Animal Diversity Web and head-appendage characters in Phenoscape.

label: Deer alone have solid horns and alone shed them
claim: Deer are the only animals whose horns are solid throughout, and the only animals that shed their horns.
quote: Deer are the only animals in which the horns are solid throughout, and are also the only animals that cast them.
measurable_quantities: horn/antler structure (solid bone versus keratin sheath over bony core)
annual shedding
candidate_data: Cranial-appendage descriptions for Cervidae, Bovidae, Antilocapridae and Giraffidae in the Animal Diversity Web and Phenoscape.

label: No horned animal has front teeth in the upper jaw
claim: No horned animal has front teeth in both jaws; the upper front teeth are lacking, because the material taken from the teeth is added to the horns.
quote: Thus it is that no animal that has horns has also front teeth in both jaws, those in the upper jaw being deficient. For nature by subtracting from the teeth adds to the horns
scope: horned mammals (bovids, deer and other ruminants)
measurable_quantities: presence of upper incisors in horned versus hornless mammal species
candidate_data: Dental formulae in the Animal Diversity Web and dental characters in Phenoscape, mapped on the Open Tree of Life.

label: Animals without a lung have no neck
claim: An animal that has no lung has no neck, the neck existing for the windpipe; fishes are an example.
quote: Therefore it is that, when there is no lung, there is also no neck. Of this condition the Fishes are an example.
measurable_quantities: presence of a lung
presence of a neck (cervical region) across vertebrate taxa
candidate_data: Cervical-region and lung characters in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase.

label: Only hairy, lunged animals have an epiglottis
claim: An epiglottis is found only in animals with blood that have a lung and a hairy skin; animals covered with scaly plates or feathers have none, the larynx itself closing instead.
quote: This part is not found in all sanguineous animals, but only in such of them as have a lung; nor in all of these, but only in such as at the same time have their skin covered with hairs, and not either with scaly plates or with feathers.
scope: animals with blood: hairy viviparous quadrupeds (mammals) versus reptiles and birds
measurable_quantities: presence of an epiglottis across vertebrate classes
candidate_data: Laryngeal anatomy in Uberon and Phenoscape, and comparative anatomy specimens in MorphoSource.

label: Only animals with blood have viscera
claim: Viscera (heart, lung, liver, spleen, kidneys) are found only in animals with blood; no bloodless animal has any viscera at all.
quote: These are peculiar to sanguineous animals, some of which have all of them, others only a part, while no bloodless animals have any at all.
scope: animals with blood (roughly vertebrates) versus bloodless animals (cephalopods, crustaceans, testaceans, insects)
measurable_quantities: presence of heart, liver/digestive gland, kidney-like organs in invertebrate taxa
candidate_data: Invertebrate organ anatomy in Uberon and the Animal Diversity Web.

label: The heart is the first part formed and at once contains blood
claim: In animals with blood the heart is the first of all the parts to be formed in the embryo, and it contains blood as soon as it is formed.
quote: For the heart is the first of all the parts to be formed; and no sooner is it formed than it contains blood.
scope: embryos of animals with blood (e.g. the chick in the egg)
measurable_quantities: order of organ formation in vertebrate embryos
timing of first heartbeat and blood in the heart
candidate_data: Embryonic staging series and developmental-stage ontologies (e.g. Hamburger–Hamilton chick stages, ZFIN zebrafish stages).

label: The heart is the source of all sensation, pain and pleasure
claim: The motions of pain, pleasure and all sensation have their source in the heart and end there; the heart, not the head, is the primary seat of sensation.
quote: Moreover, the motions of pain and pleasure, and generally of all sensation, plainly have their source in the heart, and find in it their ultimate termination.
measurable_quantities: site of sensory integration (heart versus brain) as shown by lesion or recording experiments
candidate_data: Neuroanatomy and lesion literature indexed in Europe PMC; no single dataset.

label: Heart and liver, and only these, are found in every animal with blood
claim: Every animal with blood has a heart and a liver, and these are the only two viscera invariably present in all of them.
quote: All sanguineous animals, then, need these two parts; and this explains why these two viscera, and these two alone, are invariably found in them all.
measurable_quantities: presence of heart, liver, spleen, kidneys, lung across vertebrate taxa
candidate_data: Organ presence/absence in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase across vertebrate clades.

label: Only in man does the heart lie to the left of centre
claim: In every animal except man the heart lies in the middle of the chest; in man it inclines a little to the left, to counterbalance the coldness of that side.
quote: In all animals but man the heart is placed in the centre of the pectoral region; but in man it inclines a little towards the left, so that it may counterbalance the chilliness of that side.
scope: man versus other animals with blood
measurable_quantities: lateral position of the heart in the thorax across mammals
candidate_data: Thoracic CT and dissection data in MorphoSource and veterinary anatomy references.

label: Only the horse and a kind of ox have a bone in the heart
claim: No animal has a bone in its heart except the horse and a certain kind of ox, where the large heart needs a bony support.
quote: In no animals does the heart contain a bone, certainly in none of those that we have ourselves inspected, with the exception of the horse and a certain kind of ox.
measurable_quantities: presence of a cardiac bone (os cordis) by species
candidate_data: Veterinary anatomy literature on the os cordis indexed in Europe PMC; no dedicated dataset.

label: Large animals' hearts have three cavities, smaller ones two
claim: In animals of great size the heart has three cavities, in smaller animals two, and in every animal at least one.
quote: In animals of great size the heart has three cavities; in smaller animals it has two; and in all has at least one
measurable_quantities: number of heart chambers versus body mass across vertebrates
candidate_data: Cardiac chamber counts from comparative anatomy (Uberon, Phenoscape) combined with body masses from PanTHERIA and AnAge.

label: Animals with a large heart are timid, with a small heart courageous
claim: An animal with a large heart is timid and one with a smaller, moderate heart is more courageous; the hare, deer, mouse, hyena, ass, leopard and marten have large hearts.
quote: So also when the heart is of large size the animal is timorous, while it is more courageous if the organ be smaller and of moderate bulk.
scope: animals with blood; hare, deer, mouse, hyena, ass, leopard, marten
measurable_quantities: relative heart mass (heart mass / body mass)
measures of fearfulness or flight response
candidate_data: Allometric heart-mass compilations in the comparative physiology literature, with behavioural boldness data where available; no single standard dataset.

label: Blood is the material from which the whole body is built
claim: Blood is the material from which every part of the body is made, which is why nature has laid down vessels like irrigation channels throughout the whole body.
quote: Now just after the same fashion has nature laid down channels for the conveyance of the blood throughout the whole body, because this blood is the material out of which the whole fabric is made.
candidate_data: none known

label: Breathing serves to cool; fishes are cooled by water and have gills, not a lung
claim: Animals with blood must be cooled from outside, by air or by water; fishes are cooled by water and therefore never have a lung but have gills in its place.
quote: The external cooling agent must be either air or water. In fishes the agent is water. Fishes therefore never have a lung, but have gills in its place
measurable_quantities: role of gills and lungs in heat exchange versus gas exchange
presence of lungs in fishes
candidate_data: Respiratory physiology literature and lung/gill characters in Phenoscape (lungfishes, bichirs).

label: Viviparous animals have large blood-rich lungs, oviparous ones small dry lungs
claim: In viviparous animals the lung is large and full of blood because of their natural heat, while in egg-laying animals (oviparous quadrupeds and birds) it is small, dry and spongy but can expand greatly when inflated.
quote: In the vivipara it is large and rich in blood, because of their natural heat; while in the ovipara it is small and dry but capable of expanding to a vast extent when inflated.
scope: viviparous quadrupeds (mammals) versus lizards, tortoises and birds
measurable_quantities: lung mass and vascularity relative to body mass
lung volume when inflated
candidate_data: Comparative lung morphometry in the respiratory physiology literature (Europe PMC); lung characters in Phenoscape.

label: Feathered and scaly animals lack a bladder, tortoises excepted
claim: Animals covered with feathers, scales or scaly plates have no urinary bladder, the tortoises being the only exception.
quote: all these animals, owing to the small amount of fluid which they imbibe, and owing also to such residue as there may be being converted into feathers and the like, are invariably without a bladder. The Tortoises, which are comprised among animals with scaly plates, form the only exception
scope: birds, reptiles, fishes; tortoises and turtles
measurable_quantities: presence of a urinary bladder across birds, reptiles and fishes
candidate_data: Urinary-bladder characters in Uberon and Phenoscape across reptiles, birds and fishes.

label: Feathered and scaly animals have no kidneys, tortoises excepted
claim: Kidneys are lacking in all animals clad with feathers, scales or scaly plates, the sea and land tortoises being the only exception; some birds have only flattened kidney-like bodies.
quote: For these also are wanting in all animals that are clad with feathers or with scales or with scale-like plates; the sea and land tortoises forming the only exception.
measurable_quantities: presence of kidneys across birds, reptiles and fishes
candidate_data: Kidney characters in Uberon and Phenoscape across vertebrate clades.

label: The right kidney always lies higher than the left
claim: In all animals that have kidneys, the right kidney is placed higher than the left.
quote: In all animals that have kidneys, that on the right is placed higher than that on the left.
measurable_quantities: craniocaudal position of right versus left kidney by species
candidate_data: Veterinary and human anatomical imaging data (e.g. CT scans in MorphoSource) and comparative anatomy references.

label: Man is the only animal that laughs
claim: Man is the only animal that laughs, and therefore the only animal that is affected by tickling.
quote: That man alone is affected by tickling is due firstly to the delicacy of his skin, and secondly to his being the only animal that laughs.
measurable_quantities: occurrence of laughter-like vocalisations and tickle responses in non-human animals
candidate_data: Behavioural studies of play vocalisations and tickling in apes and rats indexed in Europe PMC; no single dataset.

label: Viviparous animals with front teeth in both jaws have a single stomach
claim: The stomach is single in all viviparous animals with blood that have front teeth in both jaws, such as man, dog, lion, horse, mule, ass and pig.
quote: Thus the stomach is single in all such sanguineous and viviparous animals as have teeth in front of both jaws.
scope: viviparous quadrupeds and man with upper and lower incisors
measurable_quantities: presence of upper incisors
number of stomach chambers
candidate_data: Dental formulae and stomach morphology in the Animal Diversity Web and Phenoscape, mapped on the Open Tree of Life.

label: Horned animals have several stomachs because they lack upper front teeth
claim: Horned animals (sheep, ox, goat, deer and the like) have several stomachs, because they lack front teeth in the upper jaw and the stomachs make up for the imperfect chewing.
quote: A similar multiplicity of stomachs exists also in the horned animals; the reason being that horn-bearing animals have no front teeth in the upper jaw.
scope: horned ruminants: sheep, ox, goat, deer; also the camel
measurable_quantities: number of stomach chambers
presence of upper incisors
presence of horns
candidate_data: Stomach and dental characters in Phenoscape and the Animal Diversity Web across artiodactyls.

label: The parrot-fish alone among fishes ruminates
claim: The Scarus (parrot-fish) apparently ruminates, though no other fish does.
quote: And this is probably the reason why this fish apparently ruminates, though no other fishes do so.
measurable_quantities: regurgitation and re-chewing of food in parrot-fishes
candidate_data: Feeding-biology accounts in FishBase and the literature on the pharyngeal mill of Scaridae.

label: Rennet occurs in all multi-stomached animals and, among others, in the hare
claim: Rennet is found in all animals with a multiple stomach and, among single-stomached animals, in the hare.
quote: What is known as rennet is found in all animals that have a multiple stomach, and in the hare among animals whose stomach is single.
measurable_quantities: presence of milk-clotting enzymes (chymosin activity) in the stomachs of young ruminants and hares
candidate_data: Enzyme and gene-presence data in UniProt and Ensembl for chymosin orthologues across mammals.

label: Vipers and selachians produce eggs internally and bear live young
claim: Vipers among serpents, like the selachians (cartilaginous fishes) among fishes, first produce eggs internally and then bring forth live young.
quote: For both these and vipers are externally viviparous, but previously produce ova internally.
measurable_quantities: reproductive mode (oviparity, ovoviviparity, viviparity) by species
candidate_data: Reproductive-mode fields in the Reptile Database and FishBase.

label: All fishes have a gall-bladder, mostly attached to the intestine
claim: All fishes have a gall-bladder, and in most of them it is attached to the intestine rather than to the liver.
quote: For all fishes have a gall-bladder; and in most of them it is attached to the intestine
measurable_quantities: presence and attachment site of the gall-bladder across fish species
candidate_data: Gall-bladder characters in Phenoscape and Uberon for fishes.

label: Horse, mule, ass, deer and roe have no gall-bladder
claim: Some animals have no gall-bladder at all, among them the horse, mule, ass, deer and roe; the camel has only small biliary vessels, and the seal and dolphin have none.
quote: For in some animals there is absolutely no gall-bladder at all--in the horse, for instance, the mule, the ass, the deer, and the roe
scope: horse, mule, ass, deer, roe deer, camel, seal, dolphin
measurable_quantities: presence of a gall-bladder by species
candidate_data: Gall-bladder presence across mammals in Phenoscape/Uberon and comparative anatomy literature indexed in Europe PMC.

label: Gall-bladder size in sheep and goats varies by locality
claim: Sheep and goats usually have a gall-bladder, but in some localities (Naxos) it is enormously large and in others (a district of Chalcis in Euboea) it is altogether absent.
quote: For these animals usually have a gall-bladder; but, while in some localities it is so enormously big as to appear a monstrosity, as is the case in Naxos, in others it is altogether wanting
scope: sheep and goats in different localities
measurable_quantities: gall-bladder presence and size in sheep and goat populations by region
candidate_data: Abattoir and veterinary survey data; none known as a public dataset.

label: Animals without a gall-bladder are long-lived
claim: Animals without a gall-bladder, such as deer, solid-hoofed animals, the camel and the dolphin, are long-lived.
quote: For such have no gall-bladder and live long. But besides these there are other animals that have no gall-bladder, though those old writers had not noticed the fact, such as the camel and the dolphin; and these also are, as it happens, long-lived.
scope: mammals with and without a gall-bladder: deer, horse, ass, camel, dolphin
measurable_quantities: maximum lifespan corrected for body mass
presence of a gall-bladder
candidate_data: Maximum lifespan and body mass from AnAge and PanTHERIA, joined to gall-bladder presence from comparative anatomy.

label: All cephalopods have ink, the cuttlefish most
claim: All cephalopods have ink, and the cuttlefish (Sepia) has more of it than any other.
quote: All Cephalopoda alike have this characteristic ink, but chief of all the Sepia, where it is more abundant than in the rest.
measurable_quantities: presence and volume of the ink sac relative to body size by species
candidate_data: Cephalopod anatomy in SeaLifeBase and the cephalopod literature; ink-sac absence in some deep-sea taxa.

label: Crayfish and some crabs have a second set of teeth in the stomach
claim: In the Carabi (spiny lobsters and the like) and some crabs the stomach has a second set of teeth, because the front teeth are not enough to chew the food properly.
quote: and then a stomach, which in the Carabi and some of the Crabs is furnished with a second set of teeth, the anterior teeth being insufficient for adequate mastication.
scope: decapod crustaceans: Carabi (spiny lobsters, crayfish) and crabs
measurable_quantities: presence of a gastric mill with teeth in decapod species
candidate_data: Decapod foregut anatomy in the crustacean literature and specimen scans in MorphoSource.

label: Every sea-urchin has five 'eggs', five teeth and five stomachs
claim: The number of so-called eggs is the same in all sea-urchins and is odd: five, matching their five teeth and five stomach compartments.
quote: The number of the ova is the same in all sea-urchins, and is an odd one. For there are five ova, just as there are also five teeth and five stomachs
measurable_quantities: number of gonads
number of teeth in Aristotle's lantern
number of gut compartments
candidate_data: Echinoid anatomy in the World Register of Marine Species literature links and specimen scans in MorphoSource.

label: Sea-urchin 'eggs' grow largest at full moon
claim: The so-called eggs of sea-urchins become larger than usual at the time of the full moon, because the nights are then warmer from the moonlight, not because the urchins eat more.
quote: yet they acquire a greater size than usual at the time of full moon; not, as some think, because sea-urchins eat more at that season, but because the nights are then warmer, owing to the moonlight.
measurable_quantities: gonad index across the lunar cycle
night-time temperature across the lunar cycle
candidate_data: Gonad-index time series for echinoids (e.g. Paracentrotus lividus, Diadema setosum) in the marine biology literature.

label: Nature passes from lifeless things to animals by unbroken gradation
claim: Nature passes from lifeless things to animals in an unbroken sequence, with living things that are not animals between them, so that neighbouring groups scarcely differ.
quote: For nature passes from lifeless objects to animals in such unbroken sequence, interposing between them beings which live and yet are not animals, that scarcely any difference seems to exist between two neighbouring groups owing to their close proximity.
scope: all living things: plants, sponges, ascidians, animals
candidate_data: none known

label: Cicadas live on moisture deposited from the air
claim: Cicadas find enough to live on in the moisture deposited from the air, insects in general being small eaters because of their cold nature.
quote: In no insects is this so conspicuous as in these Cicadae. For they find enough to live on in the moisture which is deposited from the air.
measurable_quantities: food source of adult cicadas (dew versus plant xylem sap)
candidate_data: Feeding-ecology literature on Cicadidae (xylem feeding) indexed in Europe PMC.

label: Very small flying insects have only two wings
claim: Flying insects that are very small have only two wings, as flies do, while larger ones such as bees have four.
quote: When, however, such insects are of very small bulk, their feathers are reduced to two, as is the case with flies.
scope: flying insects: Diptera versus Hymenoptera and others
measurable_quantities: number of functional wings
body size across insect orders
candidate_data: Insect body-size and wing-morphology data from the insect trait literature and GBIF taxon checklists.

label: In crabs and spiny lobsters the right claw is always the larger
claim: In the Carabi (spiny lobsters and crayfish) and in crabs the right claw is invariably the larger and stronger; only in the lobster is it a matter of chance which claw is larger.
quote: In the Carabi and in the Crabs the right claw is invariably the larger and the stronger.
scope: decapod crustaceans with claws: crabs, Carabi; lobsters (Astaci) as the stated exception
measurable_quantities: proportion of individuals with the larger claw on the right, by species
candidate_data: Claw-handedness studies in decapods (e.g. Uca fiddler crabs, Cancer, Homarus) in the crustacean literature.

label: All cephalopods have eight feet, short in cuttlefish and squid, long in octopus
claim: All cephalopods have eight feet, which are short in cuttlefish and squid and longer in the octopus.
quote: Again, though the number of feet is the same in all the Cephalopoda, namely eight, their length varies in different kinds, being short in the Sepias and the Calamaries, but greater in the Poulps.
measurable_quantities: number of arms
arm length relative to mantle length
candidate_data: Morphometric data for cephalopods in SeaLifeBase and the taxonomic literature.

label: Wolves and lions have a neck made of a single bone
claim: In all other animals the neck is flexible and has several vertebrae, but in wolves and lions it consists of a single bone.
quote: In all other animals this neck is flexible and contains several vertebrae; but in wolves and lions it contains only a single bone.
scope: wolves and lions versus other animals with a neck
measurable_quantities: number of cervical vertebrae and their fusion in Canis lupus and Panthera leo
candidate_data: Skeletal specimens and CT scans in MorphoSource; cervical vertebra counts in Phenoscape.

label: Foals are nearly as tall as grown horses, with relatively long legs
claim: In solid- and cloven-hoofed quadrupeds the lower parts are largest in youth, so that foals are scarcely shorter than full-grown horses and can touch their heads with their hind legs, which adults cannot.
quote: Thus it is that colts are scarcely, if at all, below full-grown horses in height; and that while still young they can touch their heads with the hind legs, though this is no longer possible when they are older.
scope: horses and other hoofed quadrupeds; contrasted with human children, whose upper parts are largest
measurable_quantities: leg length relative to adult leg length at birth
withers height of foals versus adults
candidate_data: Equine growth curves in the veterinary literature; ontogenetic allometry studies of ungulates.

label: Man has hands because he is intelligent, not intelligent because he has hands
claim: Man does not owe his superior intelligence to his hands, as Anaxagoras held; he has hands because he is the most intelligent animal, nature giving each organ to the animal that can use it.
quote: we must conclude that man does not owe his superior intelligence to his hands, but his hands to his superior intelligence.
candidate_data: none known

label: Wolves, lions, dogs and leopards have five front toes and four hind
claim: Some polydactylous quadrupeds, such as wolves, lions, dogs and leopards, have five digits on each forefoot but only four on each hind foot.
quote: It is this hand-like office of the anterior limbs which explains why in some of the polydactylous quadrupeds, such as wolves, lions, dogs, and leopards, there are actually five digits on each forefoot, though there are only four on each hind one.
measurable_quantities: digit count on fore- and hind feet
candidate_data: Digit counts in Phenoscape and skeletal specimens in MorphoSource.

label: Mammae: two at the thighs in animals with few young, many on the belly in litter-bearers
claim: Animals that bear few young at a time, whether horned or solid-hoofed, have two mammae in the region of the thighs, while litter-bearing or polydactylous animals have numerous teats along the belly or two in the middle of the abdomen.
quote: Thus in such animals as produce but few at a birth, whether horned quadrupeds or those with solid hoofs, the mammae are placed in the region of the thighs, and are two in number, while in such as produce litters, or such as are polydactylous, the dugs are either numerous and placed laterally on the belly, as in swine and dogs
scope: viviparous quadrupeds: horse, ass, camel, deer, ox, goat, swine, dog, lion
measurable_quantities: number and position of teats
litter size
candidate_data: Teat counts and litter size in PanTHERIA, AnAge and the Amniote Life-History Database.

label: All female quadrupeds urinate backwards; only a few males do
claim: All female quadrupeds urinate backwards, while among males only a few do so, such as the lynx, lion, camel and hare; no solid-hoofed quadruped urinates backwards.
quote: All female quadrupeds void their urine backwards, because the position of the parts which this implies is useful to them in the act of copulation. This is the case with only some few males, such as the lynx, the lion, the camel, and the hare.
measurable_quantities: direction of urination by sex and species
candidate_data: Behavioural descriptions in the Animal Diversity Web and the mammalian behaviour literature.

label: Man alone lacks a tail and alone has buttocks
claim: Man has no tail but has buttocks, which no quadruped has; the nourishment that would go to a tail goes to the buttocks and fleshy legs that upright posture requires.
quote: But man is tail-less. He has, however, buttocks, which exist in none of the quadrupeds.
scope: man versus quadrupeds; the ape as intermediate
measurable_quantities: presence of an external tail
relative mass of gluteal muscles
candidate_data: Comparative primate and mammal anatomy in Phenoscape and MorphoSource.

label: Huckle-bones occur mostly in cloven-hoofed animals, never in many-toed ones
claim: No polydactylous quadruped has a huckle-bone (astragalus), solid-hoofed animals as a rule lack one, and most animals that have one are cloven-hoofed.
quote: As to the polydactylous quadrupeds, none of them have huckle-bones. For if they had they would not be polydactylous, but the divisions of the foot would only extend to that amount of its breadth which was covered by the huckle-bone. Thus it is that most of the animals that have huckle-bones are cloven-hoofed.
measurable_quantities: presence and form of the astragalus by foot type
candidate_data: Tarsal characters in Phenoscape and astragalus specimens in MorphoSource.

label: The river crocodile alone among these animals has no tongue
claim: All oviparous quadrupeds and serpents have a tongue in the mouth except the river crocodile, which has only a space where a tongue would be.
quote: and in all, with the single exception of the river crocodile, there is a tongue inside the mouth.
scope: oviparous quadrupeds and serpents; the Nile crocodile
measurable_quantities: presence and mobility of the tongue in crocodilians
candidate_data: Crocodilian oral anatomy in the herpetological literature and specimen scans in MorphoSource.

label: Oviparous quadrupeds have no upper eyelid and close the eye with the lower
claim: Oviparous quadrupeds have no upper eyelid and close the eye with the lower lid, as birds do.
quote: These animals have no upper eyelid, but close the eye with the lower lid In this they resemble birds
scope: oviparous quadrupeds (lizards, tortoises, crocodiles) and birds
measurable_quantities: presence and mobility of upper and lower eyelids
candidate_data: Eyelid characters in Phenoscape and the herpetological anatomy literature.

label: The crocodile moves its upper jaw rather than its lower
claim: In all other animals it is the lower jaw that moves, but in the river crocodile it is the upper jaw.
quote: While in all other animals it is the lower jaw that is movable, in the river crocodile it is exceptionally the upper.
scope: the Nile crocodile versus other animals
measurable_quantities: relative motion of upper and lower jaw (cranial kinesis) during feeding
candidate_data: Crocodilian jaw biomechanics studies and skull scans in MorphoSource.

label: No animal that is not internally viviparous has milk or mammae
claim: No animal that is not internally viviparous has milk or mammae, so birds, fishes, oviparous quadrupeds and serpents have none; in them the nourishment corresponding to milk is formed in the egg.
quote: This absence of milk is not peculiar to these animals, but is common to all such as are not internally viviparous.
measurable_quantities: presence of mammae or milk-like secretions by reproductive mode
candidate_data: Reproductive-mode data in the Amniote Life-History Database and literature on crop milk and monotreme lactation.

label: Long-legged birds have long necks, except web-footed birds
claim: In birds the length of the neck as a rule follows that of the legs, long-legged birds having long necks and short-legged birds short ones, with web-footed birds as the exception.
quote: For long-legged birds have a long neck, short-legged birds a short one, to which rule, however, the web-footed birds form an exception.
measurable_quantities: neck length
leg (tarsus) length
foot webbing
candidate_data: Tarsus length in AVONET, with neck length from skeletal specimens in MorphoSource.

label: Spurs and talons never co-occur in the same bird
claim: No bird has both spurs and talons; spurs belong to heavy ground birds and talons to birds of prey.
quote: Spurs and talons never co-exist in the same bird. For nature never makes anything superfluous
scope: birds: Galliformes and other spurred birds versus raptors
measurable_quantities: presence of tarsal spurs
presence of raptorial talons
candidate_data: Morphological character data in Phenoscape and species accounts in the Animal Diversity Web.

label: All birds have four toes
claim: All birds, web-footed or not, have four toes on each foot, three in front and one behind (the Libyan ostrich set aside).
quote: In all birds alike, whether web-footed or not, the number of toes in each foot is four.
measurable_quantities: number of toes per foot across bird species
candidate_data: Toe-count characters in Phenoscape and foot-type descriptions in the Animal Diversity Web.

label: Only the wryneck has two toes in front and two behind
claim: The wryneck is the only bird whose toes are arranged two in front and two behind; all other birds have three in front and one behind.
quote: The arrangement of the toes is such as has been described in all birds with the exception of the wryneck. Here only two of the toes are in front, the other two behind
measurable_quantities: toe arrangement (anisodactyl, zygodactyl, etc.) across bird species
candidate_data: Foot-type data in Phenoscape and AVONET-linked trait compilations.

label: Fishes have at most four fins
claim: Fishes that are not broad and flat have four fins, two above and two below, and no fish ever has more than four.
quote: Fishes, unless, like the Batos and the Trygon, they are broad and flat, have four fins, two on the upper and two on the under side of the body; and no fish ever has more than these.

measurable_quantities: number of paired fins per species
candidate_data: Fin characters in FishBase and Phenoscape.

label: Selachians lack gill covers because their skeleton is cartilage
claim: In most fishes the gills are covered by opercula, but selachians (cartilaginous fishes) have none, because their skeleton is cartilaginous.
quote: These gills are in most fishes covered by opercula, but in the Selachia, owing to the skeleton being cartilaginous, there are no such coverings.
measurable_quantities: presence of a bony operculum by fish clade
candidate_data: Opercular characters in Phenoscape and FishBase.

label: Selachians and the dolphin have an underslung mouth and turn on the back to feed
claim: In the dolphin and the selachians the mouth is on the underside, so they turn onto their backs to take their food.

label: No fish and no footless animal has testicles
claim: No fish has testicles, either external or internal, and neither does any footless animal, including the serpents.
quote: No fish has testicles either externally or internally; as indeed have no apodous animals, among which of course are included the serpents.
measurable_quantities: presence of testes in male fishes and snakes
candidate_data: Gonad characters in Uberon and Phenoscape.

label: The cetacean blow-hole serves to discharge sea-water taken in by the mouth
claim: Dolphins, whales and other cetaceans have no gills but have a lung, and their blow-hole serves to discharge the sea-water taken into the mouth while feeding.
quote: But dolphins and whales and all such Cetacea are without gills; and, having a lung, are provided with a blow-hole; for this serves them to discharge the sea-water which has been taken into the mouth.

what is expelled through the blow-hole
